newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Scholar says Hong Kong firms well placed.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Scholar says Hong Kong firms well placed.

text.p: Picture a throng of eager Sunday shoppers in an urban mall gleefully studying an elaborate exhibit of -- corporate annual reports.
Only in Hong Kong, said eyewitness Michael Enright, former Harvard Business School professor and a current visiting professor at Hong Kong University.
Enright, at the time consumed in his upcoming book "A Study of the Hong Kong Advantage," stopped to ask some of the shoppers why all the interest.
"They said these are the best companies in town and maybe we can learn something," Enright told Reuters in an interview.

The brazen entrepenurial spirit of Hong Kong dealmakers, many of whom claim only a beeper and cellular phone as fixed assets, distinguishes Hong Kong from other Asian countries more dependent on managerial companies, Enright said.
This do-it-yourself attitude should help Hong Kong in its effort to sustain its current high rate of growth, Enright said.

Hong Kong's future growth has been questioned by some because of its transition this July from British to Chinese rule. Enright believes Hong Kong will be aided by several international business and economic trends pinpointed in his study, co-authored by his wife Edith Scott and former journalist David Dodwell.
Geographically, Hong Kong is perfectly situated to capitalize on the recent boom of intra-Asian trade and also to play a powerful role as the defacto captial of the Chinese business community.

Hong Kong's developed infrastructure and financial markets, free-flow of information, and relatively laize-faire politics will all help it continue to attract a multitude of overseas multinational firms, Enright said.
In addition, he said, the nation's unique mix of local and overseas multinational firms has formed a symbiotic relationship which benefits all parties.

"There are literally tens of thousands of local firms that, combined with probably 7,000 overseas multinationals ... use Hong Kong as a base or hub for their regional network," he said. "The two types compete, but also support, a type of partnership."
Hong Kong ranks fourth as a leading source of foreign direct investment behind the United States, the United Kingdom and Germany, but beating out Japan, Enright noted.

The funds have three sources: Hong Kong firms investing in mainland China, U.S. and European multinationals using Hong Kong as an Asian base, and branches of Chinese firms spending on legal, financial and consulting services not readily available on the mainland.
However, a number of challenges lie on the horizon for Hong Kong.
A growing shortage of land and both blue-collar and skilled labor has pushed real estate and wage costs higher. The unemployment rate in Hong Kong currently stands at a lowly 2.5 percent, he said.

"Land costs are extremely high, if not the highest in the world in terms of central business district rentals," Enright said. "But so far it has not turned into a wholesale departure of industries to the extent there is an unemployment issue."
"The government does control how land comes on market and there is ample room to create supply by re-zoning, redeveloping and so on," he added.

The most obvious uncertainly is the July 1, 1997 transistion from more than 150 years of British rule to Chinese leadership. "The key is going to be if Hong Kong actually assumes and is able to exercise its autonomy under the basic law," he said.

As Hong Kong readies for the China yoke in the Year of the Ox, Enright said members of the nation's mobile middle- to upper-class, as a whole, have so far stayed put, willing to bet that in Hong Kong, it will remain business as usual.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1677 ))
